common_name: Rita Jane Hens and Chicks (Pearly Olive-Pink Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in spring or fall; avoid burying the crown.

directions: 'Rita Jane' forms broad, pearly olive-green rosettes flushed with pink and tipped in deep plum-purple, with wide leaves that often develop raised, warty tubercles as they mature. This older award-winning selection holds its color best with strong direct sun and lean mineral soil, fading to plainer green in shade or overly rich ground. Keep the crown dry and well drained, since standing moisture is far more damaging to this hardy alpine succulent than winter cold. Individual rosettes are monocarpic and die after flowering, but steady offsets on short stolons quickly refill any gaps in a trough, wall crevice, or rock garden.

common_name: Silverine Hens and Chicks (Silvery Pink-Edged Sempervivum)

planting.note: Set offsets on the surface of very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; this cultivar needs bright light to develop its silvery pink edging.

directions: 'Silverine' produces sharply pointed rosettes that open burgundy in spring, deepen toward purple through the season, and carry a distinctive silvery-gray sheen and pink edging along each leaf margin. Grow in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun, which sharpens the silvery highlights and keeps rosettes tight rather than lax and pale. In midsummer, mature rosettes send up a thick flowering stalk topped with clustered pink, star-shaped blooms before that rosette dies back, monocarpic as with all sempervivums. Leave the surrounding offsets undisturbed to fill the space, and avoid winter wet, which this alpine-hardy selection tolerates poorly compared to cold or drought.

common_name: Cosmic Candy Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Fuzzy Burgundy Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to bring out the fine white cilia and deepest burgundy tones.

directions: Part of the Chick Charms breeding series, 'Cosmic Candy' forms small rosettes with a deep burgundy-red outer band around a tight green center, edged with a fine tufting of white hairs that gives the whole plant a fuzzy, frosted look. Color intensifies with bright sun, cool nights, and lean mineral soil, while shade or rich soil produces looser, greener, less textured rosettes. Water sparingly and let the gritty mix dry fully between waterings, since this compact selection is especially prone to rot if kept damp through winter. Like other sempervivums it is monocarpic, but it offsets freely, forming a dense mat of chicks well suited to troughs, crevice gardens, and small containers.

planting.note: Press offsets onto very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall, keeping the crown at the soil surface.

directions: 'Lipstick' carries compact rosettes of green to bronze-green leaves tipped in a vivid red-pink blush that deepens through cooler months, giving the cultivar its name. Full sun and lean, sharply drained soil bring out the strongest tip color and keep growth tight; in shade the contrast fades and rosettes stretch. Water only after the mix has dried completely, since excess moisture around the crown is the main risk factor for rot in this and other hardy hens and chicks. Expect the classic sempervivum life cycle of monocarpic flowering rosettes replaced continuously by basal offsets, which can be divided any time during the growing season to spread the planting.

planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in bright light with some shade from the most intense afternoon sun.

directions: Emerald Ice is a patented, variegated Aeonium selection bred for its evenly concentric rosettes of green leaves broadly margined in creamy white, forming a striking geometric pattern atop a slender stem. It grows most actively in the cool, damp winter-to-spring months and rests through summer heat, when it is prone to scorch if exposed to prolonged temperatures above the mid-90s Fahrenheit. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil with bright light and light afternoon shade in hot inland climates, watering during active growth and cutting back sharply in summer dormancy. It offsets readily at the base, making division of rooted offsets the most reliable way to propagate true-to-type plants.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container succulent in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix.

directions: 'Flow' is an intergeneric hybrid between Gasteria carinata var. verrucosa and an Aloe species, combining the sturdy, dark green, white-bumped leaves of its Gasteria parent with a slightly more open, aloe-like rosette form. It stays small and slow growing, rarely exceeding about 8 inches across even after several years, which suits it to shallow pots and mixed dish gardens. Like most gasterias it tolerates lower light better than typical succulents, making it a reliable indoor plant on an east- or north-facing windowsill. Water deeply only once the gritty mix has dried completely, and expect tubular orange flowers on a tall spike when the plant is mature and well established.

common_name: Green Ice Gasteraloe (Icy Striped Gasteria-Aloe Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container succulent in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; this hybrid clumps steadily with age.

directions: 'Green Ice' was bred by crossing the warty-leaved Gasteria 'Old Man Silver' with Gonialoe variegata, producing plump, strap-like leaves in an icy green tone patterned with darker green dotting and elongated stripes. It is slow growing but eventually forms a dense clump a foot or more across as basal offsets accumulate, so allow room in the pot or bed for several years of gradual spread. Tubular flowers, red below and white above, can appear more than once a year under favorable conditions, unlike many succulents that bloom only seasonally. Keep it in bright, indirect light and fast-draining gritty mix, watering only once the soil has dried fully, since it shares its parents' tolerance for low light and vulnerability to rot from overwatering.

common_name: White Wings Gasteraloe (Variegated Gray-Green Gasteria-Aloe Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container succulent in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix.

directions: 'White Wings' is a robust Gasteria-Aloe hybrid with gray-green, tapering leaves marked by creamy white variegated striping, spotting, and pale margins that make it stand out among plainer green gasterias. It forms a compact rosette that stays under a foot across, offsetting slowly at the base to eventually form a small cluster suitable for shallow pots. Tolerant of low light, it makes an unusually forgiving houseplant for gasteria-type succulents, though brighter indirect light produces the most pronounced white variegation. Water deeply and only once the gritty mix is fully dry, and watch for tall flower stalks bearing tubular blooms above the foliage in spring or early summer.
